title: Residue generation by normalized irreducible factors
statement: Let $K\subseteq L=K(t)$ be a rational function field extension [def-pc-field-extension, def-weil-rational-function-field], let $O\subseteq L$ be a valuation subring, and put $R=O\cap K$. Assume that every element of $L^\times$ can be multiplied by an element of $K^\times$ to become a unit of $O$. Then $\kappa(O)$ is generated as a field over $\kappa(R)$ by the residues of elements $f(t)/\pi\in O^\times$ where $f\in K[t]$ is monic irreducible and $\pi\in K^\times$ is chosen so that $f(t)/\pi$ is a unit. Consequently, if $\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(R)}\kappa(O)=1$, at least one such normalized residue is transcendental over $\kappa(R)$ [def-kun-transcendence-degree]. Here $K$ is a field [def-weil-field], $K[t]$ is the polynomial ring in one indeterminate [def-weil-polynomial-ring], and a valuation subring $B$ of a field $F$ is a subring with $x\in B$ or $x^{-1}\in B$ for every $x\ne0$. Write $\mathfrak m_B=B\setminus B^\times$ and $\kappa(B)=B/\mathfrak m_B$ for its maximal ideal and residue field.

proof.text: First identify the base residue field. If $c\in K^\times$, then $c\in R^\times$ if and only if both $c$ and $c^{-1}$ belong to $R=O\cap K$, equivalently both belong to $O$, equivalently $c\in O^\times$. The valuation alternative for $O$ restricts to $K$, so $R$ is a valuation subring of $K$. Thus $\mathfrak m_R=R\cap\mathfrak m_O$, and reduction $R\to O/\mathfrak m_O$ has kernel $\mathfrak m_R$. It induces an injective field map $k:=\kappa(R)\hookrightarrow E:=\kappa(O)$. Below all constants in $k$ are viewed through this map. These assertions follow directly from the valuation-subring and residue-field definitions in the statement.

source.place: Proposition 4.3.1, proof, printed p. 28, second-stage residue-generation paragraph; expanded factorization and constant-unit argument.

proof.text: The ring $K[t]$ is Noetherian by [lem-sc-p1-polynomial-noetherian] and is an integral domain by [lem-pur-polynomial-field-pid]. Apply [lem-trf-factorization-exists] to each nonzero nonunit polynomial. Consequently every nonzero polynomial $P$ has an expression $P=a\prod_{i=1}^r f_i$ with $a\in K^\times$ and $f_i$ monic irreducible, allowing $r=0$. Here is the elementary normalization: from the coefficient multiplication rule in [def-weil-polynomial-ring], the top coefficient of a product of nonzero polynomials is the product of the two nonzero top coefficients; hence degrees add. In particular a unit of $K[t]$ is a nonzero constant. For an irreducible factor $h_i$, put $c_i=\operatorname{lc}(h_i)\ne0$ and $f_i=c_i^{-1}h_i$. This is monic and irreducible: a factorization $f_i=vw$ gives $h_i=(c_iv)w$, and multiplication by the constant unit $c_i$ preserves being a unit. Absorb the finitely many $c_i$ into $a$; for a unit polynomial take $a=P$ and the empty product.

source.place: Proposition 4.3.1, proof, printed p. 28, second-stage residue-generation paragraph; expanded factorization and constant-unit argument.

proof.text:
Let $S\subset E$ be the residues of all the units $f(t)/\pi$ specified in the statement, and let $H\subseteq E$ be the smallest subfield containing $k$ and $S$ (the intersection of all such subfields). Take $u\in O^\times$. By [def-weil-rational-function-field], write $u=P(t)/Q(t)$ with nonzero $P,Q\in K[t]$. Step 2 gives $P=a\prod_i f_i$ and $Q=b\prod_j g_j$ with $a,b\in K^\times$ and monic irreducibles $f_i,g_j$. None of $f_i(t),g_j(t)$ is zero, since $K[t]$ embeds in its fraction field. The normalization hypothesis gives $\pi_i,\rho_j\in K^\times$ such that $z_i=f_i(t)/\pi_i$ and $w_j=g_j(t)/\rho_j$ lie in $O^\times$ (take the inverse of each multiplying constant). In $L$ one has
$$u=c\,\prod_i z_i\,\prod_j w_j^{-1},\qquad c=\frac{a\prod_i\pi_i}{b\prod_j\rho_j}\in K^\times.$$
Solving this identity for $c$ expresses it as a product of units of $O$. Thus $c\in K\cap O^\times=R^\times$ by Step 1. Reduction, which preserves products and inverses of units, gives $\bar u=\bar c\prod_i\bar z_i\prod_j\bar w_j^{-1}\in H$. In particular the residual constant factor has not been dropped.

source.place: Proposition 4.3.1, proof, printed p. 28, second-stage residue-generation paragraph; expanded factorization and constant-unit argument.

proof.text: Every nonzero element $x\in E=O/\mathfrak m_O$ is the residue of some $u\in O\setminus\mathfrak m_O=O^\times$, so Step 3 gives $x\in H$. Also $0\in H$. Hence $E=H$, proving the asserted field generation. The argument includes constant rational functions and empty products. It also works with any fixed choice of a normalizing scalar for each monic irreducible: if $f(t)/\pi$ and $f(t)/\pi^{\prime}$ are both units, their ratio $\pi^{\prime}/\pi$ belongs to $K\cap O^\times=R^\times$, so their residues differ by a nonzero factor in $k$ and generate the same field.

source.place: Proposition 4.3.1, proof, printed p. 28, second-stage residue-generation paragraph; expanded factorization and constant-unit argument.

proof.text: For the consequence, assume $\operatorname{trdeg}_k E=1$ and suppose every element of $S$ were algebraic over $k$. By the statement of [def-weil-relative-algebraic-closure], the elements of $E$ algebraic over $k$ form a subfield $A$ containing $k$. It contains $S$, so $E=H\subseteq A$ by the defining minimality of $H$. Every element of $E$ would therefore satisfy a nonzero polynomial over $k$. No nonempty subset of $E$ can then be algebraically independent: choose one element of such a subset and regard its nonzero annihilating polynomial as a polynomial in that one coordinate. The supremum of cardinalities of independent subsets is consequently $0$, by [def-kun-transcendence-degree], contradicting $\operatorname{trdeg}_kE=1$. Thus some element of $S$, and hence some specified normalized irreducible residue, is transcendental.
